nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Which Splunk Enterprise component is responsible for parsing incoming data, writing events to indexes on disk, and answering search requests from a search head?
flashcards.back: The indexer parses incoming data into events, writes them to indexes on disk in bucket directories, and returns matching events to search heads during distributed search. Universal forwarders only collect and forward data (no parsing). The deployment server distributes apps and configurations to forwarders. The license manager tracks daily ingest volume against the license pool.

flashcards.front: A customer wants to forward syslog data from 500 endpoints to Splunk with the smallest possible CPU and memory footprint on each endpoint. Which forwarder type is the correct choice?
flashcards.back: The universal forwarder is a dedicated, lightweight agent — it has no UI, no search capability, and minimal parsing — designed precisely for low-overhead data collection at scale. A heavy forwarder is a full Splunk Enterprise install used when local parsing, routing rules, or filtering is required. HEC is a token-authenticated HTTP endpoint for applications, not a host agent. "Search head forwarder cluster" is not a real component.

flashcards.front: On an indexer cluster, what does a replication factor (RF) of 3 and a search factor (SF) of 2 mean?
flashcards.back: In an indexer cluster the replication factor (RF) is the number of complete bucket copies maintained across peer nodes — this protects raw data. The search factor (SF) is the number of those copies that are also kept as searchable copies (with `.tsidx` index files); SF must be ≤ RF. With RF=3/SF=2 the cluster tolerates two peer-node failures without data loss and one peer-node failure without losing immediate searchability. RF/SF describe bucket copies, not search-head counts, hot/warm retention, or event duplication.

flashcards.front: An admin needs to push a single set of inputs.conf and outputs.conf changes to 200 universal forwarders. Which Splunk role centrally manages and deploys these app bundles?
flashcards.back: The deployment server centrally distributes apps and configuration bundles to deployment clients (typically universal forwarders), grouped by `serverclass.conf` definitions that match clients by host, IP, DNS, or client name. The cluster manager (formerly master node) coordinates an indexer cluster, not forwarders. The license manager only meters ingestion. The Monitoring Console is a read-only health dashboard.

nodes.title: Microsoft 365 licensing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Microsoft 365 is sold in subscription plans that bundle productivity apps, security, and device management. MS-900 exams test which plan includes which features and the volume licensing options.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Business vs Enterprise plans — key split?
flashcards.back: Business plans (Basic/Standard/Premium) are capped at 300 users. Enterprise plans (E1/E3/E5) have no user cap and include advanced compliance and security features.

flashcards.front: What does Microsoft 365 E5 add over E3?
flashcards.back: E5 adds advanced security (Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps), advanced compliance (Purview), and Power BI Pro — roughly doubles the cost of E3.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Volume Licensing vs Microsoft 365 subscription?
flashcards.back: Volume Licensing (EA, CSP) offers negotiated pricing, centralised management, and payment flexibility for large organisations; subscriptions are per-user/month via direct or partner channels.
Office 365 is the older brand for productivity apps + cloud services. Microsoft 365 adds Windows 10/11 Enterprise licences and advanced security/compliance tools.

questions.q: In Splunk Enterprise, what is the correct lifecycle order for an index bucket from creation to deletion?
choices: Hot → warm → cold → frozen (deleted or archived)
questions.explanation: Buckets are created as hot (open and writable on the indexer's fastest storage), rolled to warm when they reach size or time limits (closed, still on hot/warm volume), then rolled to cold storage (typically slower/cheaper disk), and finally frozen — at which point Splunk deletes them by default unless `coldToFrozenDir` or `coldToFrozenScript` is configured to archive. A thawed bucket is a frozen bucket re-imported for searching; it is not part of the normal forward lifecycle.

questions.q: An admin defines the same stanza `[monitor:///var/log/nginx/access.log]` in both `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/inputs.conf` and inside an app at `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/nginx_inputs/local/inputs.conf`. Which configuration wins for that input?
choices: The app's local/inputs.conf (apps override system local)
Whichever file has the most recent modification time wins
The two settings are merged stanza-by-stanza with no winner
system/local/inputs.conf (system local has the highest precedence)
questions.explanation: Splunk's configuration file precedence (for input/index-time context) places `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/` above any app's `local/` directory. The precedence order is roughly: system/local > app/local > app/default > system/default. Modification time and "merge with no winner" are not how Splunk resolves conflicts — it picks one value per attribute based on precedence and lexical app order.

questions.q: Which Splunk configuration file is the correct place to assign a sourcetype to incoming events based on the file path, and to set line-breaking and timestamp-extraction rules for that sourcetype?
questions.explanation: `props.conf` is where source/sourcetype/host-based parsing rules live — including `LINE_BREAKER`, `SHOULD_LINEMERGE`, `TIME_PREFIX`, `TIME_FORMAT`, `MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD`, and `TRANSFORMS-*` references. `inputs.conf` only declares the data source (a monitor stanza, TCP port, scripted input, etc.). `outputs.conf` configures forwarder destinations. `transforms.conf` defines regex-based field extractions and routing rules that are invoked from `props.conf`.

questions.q: A Splunk environment ingests 480 GB on Monday against a 500 GB/day license. On Tuesday it ingests 540 GB. What happens?
choices: Tuesday's ingest is hard-blocked at 500 GB and 40 GB is silently dropped
The Monday under-use of 20 GB carries forward and absorbs the Tuesday overage
The Splunk indexers stop accepting data immediately and forwarders queue indefinitely
A license violation is recorded; after 5 violations in a rolling 30-day window, search is disabled on affected indexes
questions.explanation: Splunk Enterprise records a license violation when daily indexed volume exceeds the licensed quota. With Enterprise (free trial and dev licenses behave differently) data continues to be indexed but a warning is logged; if 5 violations occur in a rolling 30-day window (the standard threshold), search is disabled on the affected indexes until the violation is cleared or a stacking license is added. Splunk does not silently drop, hard-block ingest, or carry over unused quota.

nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

questions.q: Which component coordinates a search head cluster, including configuration replication and captaincy election among the members?
choices: The deployer (separate Splunk instance, not part of the cluster)
Any one of the search heads, dynamically promoted
questions.explanation: A search head cluster (SHC) is managed by a dedicated **deployer** — a separate Splunk instance that bundles and pushes app and configuration updates to all SHC members. The cluster itself elects a **captain** (a member, not an external node) at runtime to coordinate replication and job scheduling; that's separate from the deployer's role. The cluster manager / master node is the indexer-cluster controller, a different cluster type. The deployment server manages forwarders, not search head clusters.

questions.q: On a heavy forwarder, an admin wants to route events from sourcetype `cisco:asa` to a remote indexer group while still indexing all other data locally. Which two configuration files are required to define this routing?
choices: props.conf and transforms.conf (and outputs.conf to define the target group)
questions.explanation: Selective indexer routing on a heavy forwarder is driven by `props.conf` (which attaches a `TRANSFORMS-routing` to the sourcetype) plus `transforms.conf` (which defines a routing stanza with `DEST_KEY=_TCP_ROUTING` and `FORMAT=<target_group>`). The target group itself is defined in `outputs.conf`. `inputs.conf`/`indexes.conf` configure data collection and on-disk indexes, not routing. The `deploymentclient`/`serverclass` files manage deployment-server relationships. The `authentication`/`authorize` files configure auth and roles.

questions.q: Which Splunk role-based access mechanism controls whether a user can perform a specific action like running a real-time search, scheduling a search, or editing knowledge objects?
questions.explanation: Capabilities (such as `rtsearch`, `schedule_search`, `edit_user`, `delete_by_keyword`) are granular permissions defined per role in `authorize.conf` and inherited via role hierarchies. Index-level permissions only gate which indexes a role can search/write. The UI inactivity timeout governs idle session expiry, not action permission. App visibility flags only affect which apps appear in the UI, not what a user is allowed to do.

questions.q: A Splunk admin needs a near-real-time, browser-based view of overall environment health — indexer queues filling up, forwarder connection counts, search concurrency, and license usage. Which built-in app should they open?
questions.explanation: The Monitoring Console (MC, historically called the Distributed Management Console — DMC) is the built-in admin app that aggregates platform health metrics: indexer pipeline queues, indexing rate, forwarder connections, search-head load, license usage, KV store and clustering status. Enterprise Security and ITSI are paid premium apps focused on security analytics and service-level monitoring respectively. Splunk Stream is a wire-data capture add-on.
